newsitem.title: PERU: Freed hostage says bond with Peru rebel saved him.
newsitem.headline: Freed hostage says bond with Peru rebel saved him.

text.p: A bond of friendship with a Marxist rebel over a shared appreciation of art kept Peruvian Agricultural Minister Rodolfo Munante alive during this week's military raid, the former hostage said on Friday.

Munante, who was rescued with 70 others from the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima on Tuesday after 126 days in captivity, shared with reporters the dramatic moment when he came face-to-face with a rebel's gun.
Moments after a floor-shaking explosion signalled the start of the military assault, a teenage guerrilla entered the room where Munante and other high-ranking hostages were held.
"I turned around and there was this boy pointing his rifle at me," he told a news conference. "I looked at him and he was aiming at me but he didn't shoot."
Instead, the rebel turned his automatic rifle to the other side of the room and fired. The bullets probably killed army Lt. Col. Juan Valer, one of two army officers who died in the raid.
One hostage and all 14 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels also died in the attack.
Since that afternoon, Munante said he had turned over and over in his mind the moment when he and the rebel "looked eye to eye" over the barrel of his gun.
"I like to think he didn't kill me because there was this bond," he said.

Munante, one of two government ministers held by the MRTA, recalled how he had encouraged the young rebel to sketch. The drawings, "looked good, so I used to tell him: 'This is a real job. You could study it and then get a job in this. Practice some more'."
Despite forming a bond with some of his captors, Munante was dismissive of the MRTA's leaders and their aims.
As a young student abroad, "I, quite honestly, also thought that these people may have been freedom fighters."
But his experience living side-by-side with the band of rebels that raided a Dec. 17 cocktail party at the residence left him with a quite different impression.
Many of the teenage recruits had joined the group to run away from family problems and others had been snatched from their homes, he said.
"If (MRTA leader Nestor) Cerpa had let them, they would have left," the residence of their own accord, he said.
The day after walking away from the gutted ruins of the diplomatic mansion, Munante was back behind his desk at 8.30 a.m.
"I think that, after this, one comes out with great energy," he said. "I feel better than ever and with much more strength."

The minister said he spent his long hours of captivity drawing up a plan to boost Peru's coffee exports and worrying about how he was to meet a government target of 100 million tree plantings for its "Year of Reforestation" while imprisoned in the ambassador's home.
